title: Basement Finishing Cost in Massachusetts (2026): Real Ranges, Line by Line
metaDescription: Basement finishing cost in Massachusetts for 2026: per square foot ranges, cost by project type, and the moisture, egress and bathroom items that move it.
secondaryKeywords: basement finishing cost per square foot

faq.q: What is the average cost to finish a basement in Massachusetts?
faq.a: Most basements in Essex and Middlesex County cost about $35 to $90 per square foot to finish in 2026, so a typical 700 to 900 square foot basement lands roughly between $30,000 and $75,000. A bathroom, an egress window or moisture work push it higher.

faq.q: What is the average cost to finish a 1,000 square foot basement?
faq.a: A 1,000 square foot basement usually runs about $40,000 to $90,000 in our area, depending on finish level, whether a bathroom is added and how much moisture control the foundation needs.

faq.q: What is the most expensive part of finishing a basement?
faq.a: A bathroom is usually the biggest single item, often $25,000 to $55,000 on its own. After that come moisture and drainage work, egress windows for bedrooms, and heating or cooling the new space.

faq.q: Is finishing a basement worth the money?
faq.a: For most families, yes. It adds living space for far less per square foot than a home addition, because the foundation, roof and walls already exist. Doing it with moisture control, proper insulation and permits is what protects the value.

faq.q: How long does it take to finish a 1,000 square foot basement?
faq.a: Most projects take about 6 to 10 weeks once the permit is issued. A bathroom, an egress window or drainage work can add a few weeks.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to finish a basement in Massachusetts?
faq.a: Yes. Turning a basement into living space requires a building permit from your town, and electrical and plumbing work need their own permits pulled by licensed trades. The permit cost belongs in your estimate.

faq.q: Can I finish a basement that gets water?
faq.a: Only after the water problem is solved. Grading, gutters, cracks, a sump pump or interior drainage come first. Framing over a wet wall only hides the problem behind new drywall.
